title: Control Plane Baremetal Bootstrap, Networking & Rotation Runbook
content:
Purpose:
This runbook captures a tested, repeatable sequence for bootstrapping a private control plane on bare metal or VPC-backed private clouds, scaling the control plane, and performing key rotations (TLS, KMS keys, service account credentials) with minimal disruption. It is intentionally pragmatic: mixes Terraform module notes, preflight checks, live commands, smoke tests, and rollback guidance.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target: Redwood private control plane (control-plane services + stateful components) running in customer-managed infrastructure (bare metal racks or cloud VPC with dedicated subnets).
- Kubernetes distribution: upstream k8s (1.26–1.28 supported), with control plane installed as static pods / systemd-managed containers on master nodes.
- Nodes: at least 3 control-plane hosts for HA. Worker pools exist but are out-of-scope here except for API compatibility checks.
- Automation: Terraform modules manage networking, DNS, load-balancer objects, and initial instance provisioning. Ansible/CMD scripts perform OS-level bootstrap.
- Secrets: Primary KMS is customer-managed (Cloud KMS/HSM) or Redwood-managed KMS relay when appropriate.

Preflight checklist (must pass before any bootstrap or upgrade):
- Inventory: hostnames, IPs, rack positions, BMC access credentials.
- Networking: /24 control-plane subnet reserved, upstream NAT config validated, ACLs allow node-to-node (TCP 6443, etcd ports), LB health port open.
- DNS: control-plane FQDN pointed to LB VIP; wildcard cert path reserved.
- Time sync: NTP pool validated on all hosts (chrony/systemd-timesyncd).
- Storage: etcd persistent disks attached, LVM configured if required, stable disk labels.
- SSH & console access verified for all hosts.
- Backup: etcd snapshot taken and stored off-host, and restoration tested in a sandbox.
- Terraform state: remote backend accessible, locks working, and state backups present.

Bootstrap sequence (bare-metal -> control plane live):
1) Prepare Terraform workspace
   - Branch: private-cp/bootstrap/<customer>-<date>
   - terraform init (remote backend), terraform workspace select/create
   - Validate variables file: vars-network.tfvars, vars-provisioning.tfvars
   - Run terraform plan and review diffs with infra lead (ticket JIRA-DEPLOY-9821)

2) Provision network and LB
   - Apply networking module: creates VLANs/subnets, router rules, and LB VIP
   - Confirm LB responds on health-check path /healthz and routes to placeholder backend

3) Provision hosts (PXE/ASR or cloud images)
   - Use our provisioning module to set hostname, BMC config, user accounts, and disk partitioning
   - Run post-provision script: /opt/redwood/bootstrap.sh that installs container runtime, kubelet binary, and required kernel modules

4) Install etcd cluster
   - Use static etcd manifests pinned to tested version
   - Start etcd on all control nodes, verify quorum (etcdctl member list)
   - Take initial etcd snapshot: etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/initial-snap.db and copy to backups bucket

5) Install kube-apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler
   - Deploy static pods with certs from onboarding CA
   - Confirm API is responsive: kubectl --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf get componentstatuses

6) Bootstrapping controller addons (ingress controller, coredns)
   - Install coredns and an ingress implementation behind LB
   - Validate DNS resolution for control-plane services

7) Final validation & handoff
   - Execute smoke tests (see Tests section)
   - Collect logs, trace request path through LB -> kube-apiserver -> etcd

Terraform module notes (practical tips):
- network-vlan module inputs: cidr_block, gateway, public_route_table. Keep cidr allocation conservative; avoid /20 for small clusters.
- lb-allocator module outputs: lb_vip, lb_fqdn, lb_cert_id. Make sure LB health pool uses the same cert verification path as clients.
- host-provisioner module: exposes ssh_pub_keys (list), bmc_creds (sensitive). Use partials for per-rack overrides.
- etcd-module: accepts initial_snapshot_url and recover_mode flag. For upgrades, set recover_mode=false to avoid accidental replays.
- State management: Use locking (Dynamo/Cloud SQL) for remote state. CI runs apply with plan approval gate.

Scaling control plane (when to scale and how)
- Signals to scale: API latency > 99th percentile SLO, etcd leader CPU > 70% for sustained 5m, or planned capacity growth.
- Scaling strategy: scale control-plane hosts in odd-numbered increments (3 -> 5 -> 7) to preserve etcd quorums.
- Procedure:
  1) Add new host entries to inventory and tag with control-plane role in Terraform vars
  2) terraform apply to provision instance + LB backend update (do not immediately add to etcd)
  3) On new host: run provisioning scripts, ensure kubelet and container runtime healthy
  4) Join etcd using member add with peerURLs; wait for healthy replication (etcdctl endpoint status)
  5) Add kube-apiserver static pod to new host and let LB health checks pick it up
  6) Validate by draining a worker (no API interruption) and running synthetic traffic to measure latency impact

Certificate and KMS key rotation (zero-downtime approach):
- Rotation types: TLS (server/client CA), service account keys, KMS DEK/KEK rotation.
- Principles:
  - Double-write: deploy new certs/keys alongside old ones and switch consumers after validation
  - Stagger: rotate one availability set/rack at a time, validate, then proceed

TLS rotation procedure (example: API server certs):
1) Generate new CA signed certs in staging namespace (exts match existing CN/SANs)
2) Distribute new certs to control-plane nodes under /etc/kubernetes/new-certs
3) Update kube-apiserver manifest to include both certs (if supported) or use side-by-side listener on alternate port
4) Wait for node readiness and LB health checks to succeed using new certs via an isolated health check script
5) Switch LB to prefer new backend (or update VIP to new port) during a low-traffic window
6) Remove old certs after 48–72 hours of stable operation

KMS key rotation (customer-managed HSM):
- For envelope encryption: we keep 2 active KEKs (old/new). Procedure:
  1) Import new KEK into HSM and set as primary for DEK wrapping
  2) Run background job to rewrap recently-used DEKs over a rolling window
  3) Verify decryption on a canary dataset and then mark rotation complete in state store

Planned upgrade runbook (control plane components):
- Principle: always run upgrades first in a staging environment that mirrors the customer's topology. Upgrade control plane nodes before workers. Use canary hosts to validate.
- Version policy: support +2 minor versions from current GA; target path: 1.26 -> 1.27 -> 1.28 (example)
- Steps:
  1) Create upgrade plan doc and snapshot etcd. Notify stakeholders and set maintenance window (2 hours for small clusters, more for larger)
  2) Pick one control-plane host as canary. Cordone it from receiving a new leader if needed and schedule a maintenance window for that rack
  3) Drain non-control workloads and stop autoscalers from re-adding jobs
  4) Apply OS/kernel/security updates on canary, reboot if required, then upgrade kube binaries
  5) Run smoke tests and perf tests against canary (latency, leader elections, API throughput)
  6) If canary passes, roll the upgrade sequentially across remaining control-plane hosts with pause windows
  7) Post-upgrade: run full test suite, increase traffic gradually, monitor SLOs for 24–72h

Rollback strategy:
- If a control-plane host fails to rejoin or API SLOs break: revert manifest changes and reintroduce snapshot-based etcd restore on affected nodes.
- Always have an etcd restore runbook ready that includes: stopping kube-apiserver, restoring snapshot to clean disks, and starting etcd with initial-cluster-state=recover. Test this in sandbox monthly.

Smoke tests and validation (automated scripts)
- api-health.sh: checks API GET /healthz, /version, and list namespaces
- etcd-health.sh: validates leader exists, last index is advancing, member list healthy
- integration-smoke.py: creates namespace, deploys a small app, hits it via service and ingress
- micro-bench: 5-minute token-per-second generator to verify submission latency under light load

Maintenance windows and communication
- Standard window: 0200–0600 local rack timezone. Notify customer 72h in advance for major upgrades, 24h for rotations.
- Slack channels: #private-deploys <customer-slug>, on-call pager and SRE rotation must be tagged in message

Troubleshooting common failures:
- LB health failing after cert rotation: check cert chain & SNI match; run openssl s_client -connect <lb>:443 -servername <fqdn>
- etcd quorum loss after scale: check peerURLs and firewall rules; run etcdctl endpoint status and inspect wal dir for corruption
- Terraform apply stuck on resource lock: check remote state lock table and force-unlock only after human approval

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide on official supported kube versions and minimum etcd minor version for next fiscal year (assign: @Priya)
- Add automated canary traffic runner into CI to validate every control-plane Terraform update (ticket: JIRA-DEVOPS-273)
- Clarify expected RTO for KMS rotations with legal/compliance (assign: @Liam)

Appendix: Useful commands
- etcd snapshot: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 snapshot save /tmp/snap.db --cacert=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/etcd/server.key
- add etcd member: etcdctl member add <name> --peer-urls=https://<ip>:2380
- kube-apiserver logs: journalctl -u kube-apiserver -n 500 --no-pager
- terraform plan with varfile: terraform plan -var-file=vars-<customer>.tfvars

- Confluence: CONTROL-PLANE-OPERATIONS (internal doc)
- GitHub: github.com/redwood-inference/private-cp-terraform (modules referenced above)
- JIRA: JIRA-DEPLOY-9821 (initial onboarding ticket)
